questions.question: For the primal linear program $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, how many dual variables and how many dual constraints (apart from $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$) does its dual linear program have?
options: $n$ dual variables and $m$ dual constraints
$m+n$ dual variables and $n$ dual constraints
$m$ dual variables and $n$ dual constraints
$m$ dual variables and $m$ dual constraints

questions.question: To bound the objective of $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the $i$-th constraint $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i$ is multiplied by a weight $y_i$ and the results are added. Why must every weight satisfy $y_i\geq0$?
options: A negative weight flips $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i$, so the summed inequality need not hold.
A negative weight makes $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ negative, and an upper bound on $Z$ is never a negative number.
Without $y_i\geq0$ the system $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c}$ may have no solution, so no bound exists.
The sign condition only serves the price reading of $y_i$; the upper bound on $Z$ would hold for any real weights.

questions.question: A firm solves $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$; $b_i$ is the capacity of resource $i$, $c_j$ the revenue per unit of product $j$, $a_{i,j}$ the use of resource $i$ per unit of product $j$. A buyer offers $y_i$ per unit of resource $i$. What does the dual constraint for product $j$ express?
options: The buyer's total payment $\sum_ib_iy_i$ for all resources is at least the revenue $c_j$ of product $j$.
The prices of the resources used by one unit of product $j$ add up to at most its revenue $c_j$.
The amount of each resource used for product $j$, priced at $y_i$, stays within its capacity $b_i$.
The resources used by one unit of product $j$, valued at the offered prices, fetch at least its revenue $c_j$.

questions.question: For the primal $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, let $\boldsymbol{y}$ satisfy $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. What does the number $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ say about the primal?
options: It is a lower bound on $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ for every primal feasible $\boldsymbol{x}$, and the dual looks for the largest such bound.
It is an upper bound on $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ for every primal feasible $\boldsymbol{x}$, and the dual looks for the smallest such bound.
It is an upper bound on $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ only when $\boldsymbol{y}$ is a dual optimal solution; other feasible $\boldsymbol{y}$ give no bound.
It equals $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ at a primal optimal solution $\boldsymbol{x}$, whichever dual feasible $\boldsymbol{y}$ is chosen.

questions.question: Given $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$, $\boldsymbol{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, which extra condition on these data is needed before the dual linear program of $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ can be written down?
options: The right-hand side must satisfy $\boldsymbol{b}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, so that the slack variables give a starting corner point.
The matrix $\boldsymbol{A}$ must be square and invertible, so that the transpose $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}$ exists.
No extra condition: the dual is defined for every $\boldsymbol{A}$, $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$ of these sizes.
The primal must have a nonempty feasible region, otherwise there is nothing to bound.

questions.question: Which linear program is the dual of $\max Z=4x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+2x_2\leq8$, $3x_1+x_2\leq9$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$?
options: $\min W=8y_1+9y_2$ subject to $y_1+2y_2\geq4$, $3y_1+y_2\geq3$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$
$\min W=8y_1+9y_2$ subject to $y_1+3y_2\geq4$, $2y_1+y_2\geq3$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$
$\min W=4y_1+3y_2$ subject to $y_1+3y_2\geq8$, $2y_1+y_2\geq9$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$
$\min W=8y_1+9y_2$ subject to $y_1+3y_2\leq4$, $2y_1+y_2\leq3$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$

questions.question: For $\max Z=3x_1+4x_2$ subject to $x_1+2x_2\leq10$, $x_1+x_2\leq6$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, the weights $\boldsymbol{y}=(1,2)$ satisfy the dual constraints $y_1+y_2\geq3$, $2y_1+y_2\geq4$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which upper bound on $Z$ over the feasible region do these weights prove?
options: $Z\leq26$
$Z\leq11$
$Z\leq16$
$Z\leq22$

questions.question: A linear program in one variable reads $\max Z=3x$ subject to $2x\leq8$, $x\leq3$, $x\geq0$. What is its dual linear program?
options: $\min W=8y_1+3y_2$ subject to $2y_1+y_2\geq3$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$
$\min W=8y_1$ subject to $2y_1\geq3$, $y_1\geq0$
$\min W=8y_1+3y_2$ subject to $2y_1\geq3$, $y_2\geq3$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$
$\min W=3y$ subject to $2y\geq8$, $y\geq3$, $y\geq0$

questions.question: For $\max Z=x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1-x_2\leq2$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, which statement about its dual linear program is correct?
options: It has optimal value $2$, attained at $y=1$.
It has optimal value $0$, attained at $y=0$.
It has no feasible point at all.
It is unbounded below, so it has no optimal value.

questions.question: The dual of $\max 6x_1+5x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq5$, $3x_1+2x_2\leq12$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$ is $\min 5y_1+12y_2$ subject to $y_1+3y_2\geq6$, $y_1+2y_2\geq5$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$. Which vector $\boldsymbol{y}$ is feasible for this dual?
options: $\boldsymbol{y}=(-1,3)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(0,2)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(1,1)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(1,2)$

questions.question: In $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the first constraint $\boldsymbol{a}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_1$ is replaced by the equivalent $2\boldsymbol{a}_1^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq2b_1$, which leaves the feasible region unchanged. How does the dual linear program change?
options: Only the objective coefficient of $y_1$ doubles, to $2b_1$, so every dual bound $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ with $y_1>0$ gets larger.
Every coefficient of $y_1$ doubles; substituting $y_1=\tfrac{1}{2}y_1'$ gives back the old dual, so both prove the same bounds.
It does not change: the dual is determined by the feasible region of the primal, not by how its constraints are written.
Every coefficient of $y_1$ doubles, so each dual feasible $\boldsymbol{y}$ now proves a bound that is twice as large as before.

questions.question: For $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}\}$ (rows $\boldsymbol{a}_k^{\top}$ of $\boldsymbol{A}$), $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ and $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, $V$ lies in $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon(\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y})^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\}$. When is $\boldsymbol{p}$ on its boundary hyperplane?
options: $y_k=0$ for every $k$ whose constraint is slack at $\boldsymbol{p}$, that is, $\boldsymbol{a}_k^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}<b_k$
$y_k>0$ for every $k$, so that all constraints of $V$ contribute to the normal vector $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$
$\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c}$ for an objective vector $\boldsymbol{c}$, so that $\boldsymbol{y}$ is dual feasible
$y_k=0$ for every $k$ whose constraint is binding at $\boldsymbol{p}$, that is, $\boldsymbol{a}_k^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=b_k$

questions.question: For $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, call $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ a single-constraint bound if $\boldsymbol{y}$ is dual feasible with one nonzero entry. If such $\boldsymbol{y}$ exist and the dual has an optimal solution, how does its optimum compare with the best such bound?
options: It always equals the best single-constraint bound, since at an optimal corner point exactly one constraint is binding.
It is at least the best single-constraint bound, since mixing several constraints weakens each of them.
It equals the sum of the single-constraint bounds, since the dual adds up the constraints with their weights.
It is at most the best single-constraint bound and can be strictly smaller, since the dual allows any nonnegative mix.

questions.question: Before dualizing, $\max Z=3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq5$, $x_1-2x_2\geq-4$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$ is brought into standard form. Which linear program is then its dual?
options: $\min W=5y_1-4y_2$ subject to $y_1+y_2\geq3$, $y_1-2y_2\geq2$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$
$\min W=5y_1+4y_2$ subject to $y_1+y_2\geq3$, $y_1-2y_2\geq2$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$
$\min W=5y_1+4y_2$ subject to $y_1-y_2\geq3$, $y_1+2y_2\geq2$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$
$\min W=5y_1-4y_2$ subject to $y_1-y_2\geq3$, $y_1+2y_2\geq2$, $y_1,y_2\geq0$

questions.question: For $\max Z=4x_1+6x_2$ subject to $x_1+3x_2\leq9$, $2x_1+x_2\leq8$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, only the first constraint is used, with a weight $y_1\geq0$ (so $\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,0)$). What is the smallest upper bound on $Z$ that can be proved this way?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2\leq8,\ 3x_1+x_2\leq9\}$, $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,3)$ and weights $\boldsymbol{y}=(4,1)$ on the two constraints. Which equation describes the hyperplane $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon(\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y})^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\}$, which supports $V$ at $\boldsymbol{p}$?

For $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, when is $\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{0}$ feasible for the dual linear program, and what does it then show about the primal?
options: Exactly when $\boldsymbol{b}\leq\boldsymbol{0}$; it then shows that the primal has no feasible point.
Never, since a dual feasible $\boldsymbol{y}$ needs $y_i>0$ for at least one constraint to give a bound.
Always, since $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ allows zero; it shows that $Z\leq0$ for every linear program.
Exactly when $\boldsymbol{c}\leq\boldsymbol{0}$; it then shows that $Z\leq0$ at every primal feasible point.

questions.question: A student replaces $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c}$ by $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{c}$ in the dual of $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, leaving the rest of the dual unchanged. Which statement about this change is correct?
options: Its feasible weights give invalid bounds, because the bounding argument needs strict inequalities $(\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y})_j>c_j$.
It always gives the same optimal value, because at a dual optimal solution every dual constraint holds with equality.
Its bounds are still valid but the best bound can be lost, because $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ makes larger coefficients harmless.
It is needed for a valid bound, since $(\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y})_j>c_j$ and $x_j>0$ push $\boldsymbol{y}^{\top}\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}$ below $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$.

questions.question: For $\max Z=2x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1\leq4$, $x_1+x_2\leq9$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, a student writes the dual constraints as $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c}$, that is, $y_1\geq2$, $y_1+y_2\geq3$, and takes $\boldsymbol{y}=(3,0)$ with $W=\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=12$. Which conclusion about $W=12$ is correct?
options: $W=12$ is a valid upper bound on $Z$, because $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ is all that the bounding argument needs.
$W=12$ is not an upper bound on $Z$: the feasible point $(x_1,x_2)=(0,9)$ gives $Z=27$.
$W=12$ is a valid upper bound on $Z$, because $\boldsymbol{A}$ and $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}$ contain the same entries.
$W=12$ is a valid upper bound on $Z$, but not the best one, because the weight $y_2=0$ wastes a constraint.

questions.question: What is the optimal value of the dual of $\max Z=5x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq4$, $2x_1+x_2\leq6$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$?
